extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evidentiary standards for challenging, enforcing and defending IPRs in South Africa (including criminal counterfeiting complaints, civil proceedings, evidence collation and customs recordal). Focused guidance for practitioners handling IPR disputes and anti-counterfeiting actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and disbursements
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs are based on tariffs provided in the court rules; attorneys charge clients based on these tariffs or negotiated fees. Disbursements, such as court fees, counsel fees and expert witnesses, are included in costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South African courts usually award party-and-party costs (based on court tariffs, not actual negotiated costs). Other awards include attorney-and-client costs (which may exceed tariff rates) and attorney-and-own client costs (exceptional), with punitive costs in rare cases. Negotiated fees commonly apply to IPR litigation such as IPR protection and enforcement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of proceedings — application (motion) proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Application proceedings: Where there is no dispute of fact. Evidence is contained in affidavits, and ordinarily no oral evidence is heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dispute of fact arises, the matter may be referred for oral evidence. Applications are appropriate when factual disputes are unlikely or can be dealt with without oral testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of proceedings — action (trial) proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Action proceedings: Where a dispute of fact exists or is likely to arise. Evidence is given by expert witnesses in the form of oral evidence; further evidence may be led by way of affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses are examined and cross-examined. Action proceedings commence by issuing summons supported by particulars of claim that set out essential claims and material facts relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition proceedings (trade marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark application, once accepted, is advertised for opposition purposes. Any interested party may, within three months from the date of advertisement, oppose the trade mark application to prevent registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition term can be extended: first extension granted automatically via IPOnline; further extensions may be granted with applicant consent or on application to the Registrar if good cause is shown. Opposition proceedings are lodged before the Registrar and can be transferred to the High Court at any stage (including once pleadings are closed). Grounds for opposition are set out in Section 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and procedure for cancellation (revocation) proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Once registered, the validity and scope of protection of an IPR can be attacked on various grounds, resulting in cancellation, partial cancellation, or limitation of the rights afforded by the IPR registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation proceedings target the state of the register and may be pursued after registration to limit or remove rights; procedures vary by IPR type and relevant Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available civil remedies for IPR infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief available in infringement proceedings includes: an interdict; delivery up of infringing products or removal of the infringing IPR; an enquiry into damages; payment of a reasonable royalty in lieu of damages; costs; and any further or alternative relief deemed appropriate by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may craft remedies appropriate to the infringement and circumstances; remedies can be combined as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum and jurisdiction for IP disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa does not have specialised IP courts (other than the Court of the Commissioner of Patents). Formal IP disputes are heard in the High Court as court of first instance; certain matters may be heard in specialised tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of Commissioner of Patents: first instance for patent validity and infringement with nationwide jurisdiction (same authority as single judge of High Court). High Court: first instance for trademarks, copyright, design disputes. Supreme Court: appeals (except constitutional matters). Constitutional Court: where constitutional issues arise. Other forums: Trade marks Tribunal (Registrar), Copyright Tribunal, Companies Tribunal — each has defined subject-matter jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collation of evidence for IPR proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Collation of evidence confirming validity of IPRs and proof of infringement is critical. Consider any expert evidence required and identify the person best suited to provide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be compiled and retained systematically to support validity and infringement claims; consideration of who can provide credible expert testimony is essential when planning proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of validity of registered IPRs (records and renewals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration and applicable renewal certificates of IPRs must be securely retained as proof of validity and enforceability. Renewal dates must be recorded and the relevant IPR renewed within applicable time frames to avoid lapsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certificates are issued by the applicable registry (patents, designs, trade marks, certain copyrights). Maintain secure records and calendar renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of copyright subsistence and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright subsists automatically without registration. It is essential to keep proper records of how the copyright was created, details of the creator(s), job descriptions, and the date the work was created/first published. Retain a sample of the work and supporting evidence to form a library of works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed creation records strengthen proof of ownership and are important for enforcement and valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright assignment for commissioned works
rubrics_metrics.description: Where works are commissioned and the commissioner intends to retain ownership, a written copyright assignment agreement must be entered into at the time the work is created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assignment must clearly identify the work, be in writing, and be signed to be valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of common law trade mark rights (first-to-use system)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa follows a first-to-use trade mark system; proof of goodwill and reputation acquired through use must be retained to establish common law rights and sustain a passing-off claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record evidence of actual use to avoid cancellation for non-use; maintain documentation showing use in business (sales, advertising, enquiries, web traffic, product trials, consumer reports, market survey reports, awards). Update records annually as part of IP management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence types to demonstrate reputation and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of product trials and testing, sales figures, advertising spend and promotional material and brochures (including spill-over advertising), website traffic, product enquiries, consumer reports, market survey reports, awards and accolades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is not exhaustive; retain any records confirming reputation in the business and brand and update annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceable trade secret requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade secret can only be enforced if it: (1) comprises confidential information known only to a restricted number of persons; (2) is applicable in trade and industry; and (3) has economic and business value to the enforcing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrets are often part of staff know-how; codify know-how confidentially and ensure staff obligations in employment agreements (confidentiality, trade secret, and possibly restraint clauses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to secure and maintain confidentiality for trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective measures must be taken to secure and maintain confidentiality, with limited access provided only to key parties. Non-disclosure or confidentiality agreements must be kept on record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codification of know-how (SOPs, data, formulas, processes, lab notebooks, contracts) is important. Responsibility for codification and security should be enforced contractually and operationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP recordkeeping responsibility and annual audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign an identified manager to keep records of registration and use of IPRs. An annual audit should be conducted to assess validity of IPRs, attend to renewals and update internal records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper records save time and money when taking legal steps, and they are important for brand valuation and business value assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of counterfeiting under the Counterfeit Goods Act (CG Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeit Goods Act (37 of 1997) combats trade in counterfeit goods and prohibits counterfeiting. Counterfeit goods are colourable imitations substantially identical to the IPR owner's protected goods featuring the IPRs. Counterfeiting includes trade mark counterfeiting, copyright piracy, and unauthorised use of prohibited marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CG Act remedies are alternative or additional to those under the Trade Marks Act and Copyright Act. Definitions of counterfeiting, counterfeit goods, IPRs and protected goods are in Section 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark counterfeiting vs trade mark infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade mark counterfeiting applies to marks that are identical or colourable imitations of the protected trade mark. Trade mark infringement is broader and covers identical or confusingly similar marks likely to confuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade mark infringement is generally not a criminal offence in South Africa, except where it amounts to counterfeiting of products under the CG Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright piracy and criminal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright piracy is the unauthorised reproduction or distribution of copyrighted material without the owner's permission (online or in the market). Copyright infringement can be a criminal offence where the wrongdoer had guilty knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal penalties under the Copyright Act apply when the offender was aware the work was protected and that their acts were infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited marks and unauthorised use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited marks are marks declared by the Minister by notice under Section 15 of the Merchandise Marks Act. Unauthorised use of prohibited marks may be absolutely or conditionally prohibited; examples include CIPC logo, Protea Device, Olympic logo, WWF Panda, FIFA World Cup, and certain stadium representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or reproduction contrary to the notice can give rise to offences under the CG Act and related legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited activities dealing in counterfeit goods (Section 2(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(1) prohibits: possession of counterfeit goods in the course of trade for the purpose of dealing; manufacture/production other than private/domestic use; selling, hiring, bartering, offering or exposing for sale; exhibitions for trade; distribution for trade resulting in prejudice to IPR owner; importing/exporting other than private/domestic use; or any other manner disposing of in the course of trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated activities form the statutory list of prohibited dealings in counterfeit goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of the offence (intent or negligence) under Section 2(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 2(2), dealing in counterfeit goods is an offence if at the time of the conduct the person knew or had reason to suspect the goods were counterfeit (intent), or failed to take reasonable steps to avoid dealing in counterfeit goods (negligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors must establish either guilty knowledge or negligent failure to avoid the dealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may lay a Section 3 complaint and definition of Inspector
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person with an interest in the protected goods (owner, licensee, importer, exporter, distributor, authorised agent/representative/attorney) who reasonably suspects an offence related to dealing in counterfeit goods may lodge a complaint affidavit under the CG Act with any Inspector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspector includes any person appointed/designated under Section 22, any police official rank sergeant or higher, Commissioner for Customs and Excise, and officials performing Section 15 functions for goods imported into South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 complaint checklist (required contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist items for a Section 3 complaint: show rights and title in the IPR or interest in protected goods (or proof of authority if representative); provide evidence confirming IPR is valid and in force; provide details of the original goods; furnish particulars showing goods are prima facie counterfeit; establish reasonable suspicion that an offence under Section 2(2) has/ is/ will be committed; provide a sample/specimen of counterfeit goods or distinctive feature details; evidence confirming infringement; set out contraventions of the CG Act relied upon and relief sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Section 3 CG Act requirements when preparing a complaint to ensure Inspectors accept and act on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector's powers and preconditions to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Once satisfied complainant is entitled to lodge complaint, goods are prima facie protected goods, the IPR prima facie subsists, and the suspicion is reasonable, the Inspector may take appropriate steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers include searching, detaining and seizing suspected counterfeit goods, and collecting evidence as set out in Section 4. The inspector may only act with authority of a warrant under Section 6 and within the extent of powers in Section 5(1), except where warrantless action is permitted under Section 5(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrantless actions and confirmation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An Inspector can search, seize and detain counterfeit goods without a warrant under Section 5(2) if there are reasonable grounds to believe an act of dealing in counterfeit goods is being committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any act performed without a warrant must be confirmed by a Magistrate or Judge of the High Court within 10 working days; otherwise all seized goods must be returned and damages made good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage of seized counterfeit goods and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon seizure, counterfeit goods must be stored in a counterfeit goods depot. Costs of storage are paid by the IPR owner in their capacity as complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goods remain in storage until a release notice is issued by the Inspector after finalising civil/criminal proceedings or an undertaking is secured from the suspect. Storage costs can be claimed from the suspect when instituting civil proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release notice — destruction or return of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The release notice authorises destruction of goods where confirmed counterfeit, or return of goods to the suspect where time periods have not been complied with or goods are not found counterfeit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors issue release notices following procedures and confirmations during enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs recordal and Section 15 border measures
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs can be protected at the border against importation/exportation of counterfeit goods provided the IPR owner has registered with customs for such protection. Section 15 allows the owner to apply to the Commissioner for Customs and Excise to seize and detain counterfeit goods entering the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application is called a Section 15 Application (form SC-CC-01-A1) and is forwarded to the National Coordinator: Counterfeit Goods. Customs recordal enables seizure/detention of goods at the border.
